This is the performance companion to the [wall-bounded turbulence example](../../examples/wall-bounded-turbulence/index.qmd),
which is about *reproducing* the Moser–Kim–Mansour channel-flow statistics. The question here is
different: **what does that DNS actually cost across many GPUs, and what sets the limit?**

The instrument, the machine and the methodology are shared with the
[parallel-scaling study](../parallel-scaling/index.qmd) — same per-phase timers, same
Snellius `gpu_h100` partition, same one-rank-per-GPU binding with GPU-aware MPI. What changes is the
physics: walls instead of periodicity everywhere. That turns out to matter more than anything about
the hardware.

## How you scale a DNS

A periodic benchmark scales by **tiling**: add GPUs, add copies of the same vortex, and every rank
keeps solving an identical problem. A channel cannot do that. It has walls in the wall-normal
direction, so the only way to grow it is to make the box longer — which introduces ever longer
pressure modes — or to **refine** it, which is what a DNS user actually wants: more GPUs buy a finer
resolution of the *same* channel.

So the ladder here refines a fixed physical box, holding ~46 M cells per GPU:

| GPUs | grid | Δ⁺ | Mcells | Mcells/GPU |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 960 × 160 × 320 | 2.25 | 49.2 | 49.2 |
| 2 | 1152 × 192 × 384 | 1.88 | 84.9 | 42.5 |
| 4 | 1536 × 256 × 512 | 1.41 | 201.3 | 50.3 |
| 8 | 1920 × 320 × 640 | 1.13 | 393.2 | 49.2 |
| 16 | 2304 × 384 × 768 | 0.94 | 679.5 | 42.5 |
| 32 | 4096 × 512 × 704 | 0.70 | 1476.4 | 46.1 |

Rungs 1–16 are a 12H × 2H × 4H box (against MKM's 12.57 × 2 × 4.19). Every dimension is rich in
factors of two, which is not cosmetic — see [below](#grid-dimensions-are-the-single-biggest-lever).
Cells per GPU cannot be held exactly constant, because refining in three dimensions moves the cell
count in 8× steps, so weak efficiency is computed from **throughput per GPU**, which corrects for the
±8 % swing exactly.

**16 GPUs is the ceiling for a properly proportioned channel**, and it is structural rather than a
queue limit: the wall-normal direction cannot be decomposed (a no-slip wall plus an internal block
boundary decouples the two halves at the centreline), so the partitioner has only the streamwise–
spanwise plane to cut, and by 32 ranks the blocks are cube-like enough that the next bisection would
take the wall-normal axis. The 32-GPU rung therefore uses a longer 16H box, and is a slightly
different problem — read it as such.

## The curve

![Weak scaling of the channel DNS on Snellius H100, ~46 M cells/GPU. Efficiency is per-GPU throughput, so it is unaffected by the ±8 % variation in cells per GPU.](weak_scaling.png)

| GPUs | ms/step | pressure iters/step | Mcell/s | weak efficiency |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 237 | 6.0 | 207 | 100 % |
| 2 | 221 | 6.0 | 385 | 93 % |
| 4 | 322 | 7.6 | 625 | 75 % |
| 8 | 410 | 9.2 | 959 | 58 % |
| 16 | 482 | 12.9 | 1411 | 43 % |
| 32 | 700 | 18.6 | 2110 | 32 % |

**2.1 Gcell-updates/s on 32 H100s — at 32 % weak efficiency.** That is a far weaker curve than the
periodic case on the same machine, and the per-phase data says exactly why.

## Where the step goes

![Per-phase breakdown (rank-max) and the two candidate explanations: iteration count and global reductions.](channel_phases.png)

The step is 83–85 % **pressure projection** at every rank count. Everything else is flat: the
predictor holds at 20–23 ms from 1 to 32 GPUs, and the momentum solve grows only from 39 to 77 ms.

**Communication is not the bottleneck.** The pressure solve's global reductions cost 0.1 ms at 1 GPU
and 5.4 ms at 32 — **0.03 % to 0.77 % of the step**, inter-node included. Nothing in this curve is a
latency problem, and no amount of reduction-avoidance would move it.

## What actually limits it

The pressure iteration count goes **6.0 → 18.6**, a factor 3.1. Weak efficiency goes 100 % → 32 %, a
factor 3.1. The curve *is* the iteration count; there is nothing else in it.

That leaves one question worth answering: is the solve getting harder because of the **decomposition**
(more ranks) or because of the **problem** (a finer grid)? A weak-scaling ladder changes both at once,
so it cannot tell you. Running one fixed grid on more and more GPUs can:

| GPUs on a fixed 384 × 240 × 503 box | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| pressure iters/step | 24.68 | 25.77 | 24.20 | 23.85 |

**Flat.** Convergence does not depend on how the domain is cut — the distributed multigrid is doing
its job. So the growth along the ladder is the *problem* getting harder: each rung is a finer
discretisation of the same channel, and the pressure solve on a wall-bounded domain is not perfectly
resolution-independent.

This is the honest reading of the 32 % figure: the 32-GPU run is not leaving two thirds of the machine
idle, it is solving a substantially harder linear system than the 1-GPU run. It is also the difference
from the periodic benchmark, which holds **4.00 iterations at every rung from 1 to 32 GPUs and 90 %
efficiency** ([details](../parallel-scaling/index.qmd#multi-gpu-weak-scaling-132-h100-three-codes)).
Tiling a periodic box replicates a problem of fixed difficulty; refining a walled one does not. A
channel is simply a harder thing to weak-scale, and a benchmark that reports otherwise is usually
measuring the easier question.

## Grid dimensions are the single biggest lever

The pressure multigrid coarsens each axis independently, and only while that axis is **even**. An
axis's usable depth is therefore its number of factors of two — nothing to do with how large it is —
and **an odd dimension never coarsens at all**, so no coarse grid ever sees an error mode along it.

Measured on one GPU, 384 × 128 × N, everything else held fixed:

| spanwise cells | halvings | pressure iters/step | ms/step |
|---|---|---|---|
| 256 | 8 | **5.0** | 120 |
| 250 | 1 | 9.8 | 195 |
| 255 | **0** | **16.2** | **329** |

One odd number costs 3.2×, with no MPI involved at all. The effect compounds at scale — the same
channel box with 503 spanwise cells against 512:

| | 1 GPU | 8 GPUs |
|---|---|---|
| 503 cells (odd) | 830 ms, 24.7 iters | 2612 ms, 80.0 iters |
| 512 cells | 390 ms, 10.1 iters | 748 ms, 21.8 iters |
| | **2.1× faster** | **3.5× faster** |

A channel box derived the natural way — `nx = round(2π·ny)`, `nz = round(2π/3·ny)` — lands on numbers
like 1508 × 240 × 503, where the streamwise axis halves twice, the wall-normal four times, and the
spanwise never. **Round the grid to numbers rich in factors of two before anything else.** It is free,
and it is worth more than any solver option on this page.

`flow` ships a checker for this, which needs neither a GPU nor a job:

```bash
python scripts/check_decomposition.py --grid 1508,240,503 --levels 5 --np 4 --walls --verbose
```

It reports the per-axis halvings, the block each rank gets, the load imbalance, and how many multigrid
levels the hierarchy actually reaches.

## Strong scaling: the same DNS, faster

The complementary question — fixed problem, more GPUs — on the 46.4 M-cell box:

| GPUs | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ms/step | 830 | 486 | 301 | 227 |
| speed-up | 1.00× | 1.71× | 2.75× | 3.66× |
| efficiency | 100 % | 85 % | 69 % | 46 % |
| Mcells/GPU | 46.4 | 23.2 | 11.6 | 5.8 |

3.7× on 8 GPUs, with the per-GPU problem down to 5.8 M cells. The efficiency falls because the local
work shrinks toward the fixed per-step overheads, not because of the pressure solve — iterations are
flat across this sweep, as the table above shows.

## Solver options at scale

The coarse levels of a distributed geometric multigrid cannot get coarser than roughly one cell per
rank, so an **agglomerated bottom solve** is the natural lever at high rank counts. Measured on the
top two rungs:

| | 16 GPUs | 32 GPUs |
|---|---|---|
| default | 482 ms, 12.85 iters | 700 ms, 18.62 iters |
| agglomerated bottom | 461 ms, 12.85 iters | 668 ms, 17.10 iters |
| | −4.3 % | −4.5 % |

Real but small: it recovers a few percent, not the missing factor of three. The coarse-grid bottom is
not where this curve is lost, which is consistent with the hierarchy reaching 7–8 levels and a
few-thousand-cell coarsest grid at every rung.

## Reproducing

The run pack is [`benchmarks/channel-scaling/snellius/`](https://github.com/computational-chemical-engineering/peclet-examples/tree/main/benchmarks/channel-scaling/snellius)
— one job per rung, resumable, mode and result tag as positional arguments:

```bash
sbatch --nodes=4 chan_weak_gpu.sh refine        # the ladder, 1-16 GPUs
sbatch --nodes=8 chan_weak_gpu.sh refine:32     # the long-box rung + the agglomerated-bottom lever
sbatch --nodes=2 chan_weak_gpu.sh strong        # fixed-box strong scaling
```

Every run writes a JSON with the per-phase timers, iteration counts, reduction time and count, and the
full block map; all of them are in [`results/snellius-h100/`](https://github.com/computational-chemical-engineering/peclet-examples/tree/main/benchmarks/channel-scaling/results/snellius-h100),
and `plot_scaling.py` regenerates both figures from them. The driver is the production DNS driver
[`channel_dns_mpi.py`](../../examples/wall-bounded-turbulence/channel_dns_mpi.py) — the benchmark runs
the same code path as a real run, not a stripped-down kernel.
